The Ottoman steam bath: marble slab, scalding air, and an attendant who exfoliates you like a rug. You emerge two layers newer.
The spa the Romans built in Britain and named the whole town after. The waters still steam; swimming is now forbidden, which would baffle every original customer.
Japan's neighbourhood bathhouse, with a painted Mount Fuji on the wall and strict pre-wash etiquette. The tattoo rules have their own history.
The Russian steam bath where friends beat each other with birch branches, on purpose, for circulation, and then discuss it in the snow.
Korea's 24-hour spa: kiln saunas, sheep-horn towel hats, boiled eggs, and entire families asleep on heated floors at 3am.
Iceland's milky-blue geothermal spa, fed by a power station and defended by silica mud masks. The water is 39°C; the air is a rumour.
A felt hat worn in the sauna, because your ears cook before the rest of you. Looks ridiculous; works completely; the Russians stopped explaining long ago.
The ancient default: Greek athletes competed bare, and 'gymnastics' still says so. Modern sport re-invented it as the halftime streaker.
A thousand years of games at Olympia, competed in the nude, with an eternal flame and a sacred truce. Married women were banned from watching; priestesses had front-row seats.
Greek for 'naked philosophers' — the ascetics of India whom Alexander's men met and could not out-argue. They found clothes, like conquest, unnecessary.
An early sect who worshipped nude to reclaim Eden. Repeatedly suppressed, repeatedly re-founded — the idea, like the outfit, is very easy to copy.
The French 'naked city' — a resort town where tens of thousands bank, shop and dine unclothed. The supermarket trolleys are the same; everything else is negotiable.
Vancouver's seven kilometres of clothing-optional shoreline, guarded by 400 steps that filter out the merely curious.
Photographs thousands of volunteers nude in public spaces — plazas, glaciers, opera houses. Arrested five times in New York; the Supreme Court sided with the art.
Three days of peace, music, rain, and a great deal of unscheduled nudity. Half a million people; the fence never stood a chance.
A Victorian wardrobe on wheels, rolled into the sea so ladies could swim unseen. Modesty engineering's most elaborate hour.
The censor's mosaic — squares over whatever the broadcaster panicked about. The blur that admits exactly what it hides.
As old as the camera itself — the daguerreotype was invented in 1839 and the first nude studies followed within months. Humanity did not hesitate.
Portraits in lingerie and lamplight, usually a gift for exactly one recipient. The photographer's real skill is making the client laugh first.
The ancient gesture of lifting the skirt — used in folklore to repel demons, storms and enemy armies. The original flash of power.
Skipping the underwear entirely. Named for soldiers, practised universally, admitted rarely, and statistically peaking on laundry day.
Freikörperkultur — 'free body culture' — Germany's proudly organised nudism, with designated park lawns and a century of paperwork. Nudity, but with rules, which is the most German sentence possible.
The legal movement for equal shirtlessness. The courts keep discovering that the anatomy is identical and the statutes are not.
The oldest way to make a crowd look: from Godiva's tax ride to modern demonstrations. Skin, it turns out, is the one banner police cannot confiscate.
The anonymous professional whose body appears when the star declines. Film credits' politest open secret.
The first Saturday in May, annually, really. Participants recommend sunscreen, kneeling pads, and very careful rose pruning.
Japan's naked festivals: thousands of men in loincloths battling for sacred sticks in midwinter. The 1,250-year-old one recently admitted women; the temperature did not warm up.
Kawasaki's 'Festival of the Steel Phallus' — a Shinto celebration with a mikoshi you can picture, candy you can guess, and proceeds to HIV research. Entirely real, entirely cheerful.
The sumo wrestler's nine-metre silk belt and entire wardrobe. Grabbing it is legal, losing it is a disqualification, and washing it is traditionally considered bad luck.
Clothing's minimum viable product, worn from Ötzi to Tarzan. Five thousand years on the bestseller list.
Japan's traditional loincloth — standard underwear until the 1940s, now festival wear and the correct answer to 'what are they wearing at Hadaka Matsuri'.
The Pacific's swishing icon. Tourist versions are plastic; the real hula wears far more layers than the postcard promised.
Rudi Gernreich's 1964 topless swimsuit — half a bikini as a political statement. It sold 3,000 units to people who mostly never wore them outdoors.
The bikini after subtraction had gone as far as physics allows. Structural engineering's boldest sub-field.
Hair removal by hot wax and betrayal. The strip comes off faster than the vocabulary that follows it.
Andersen's tale of the finest outfit never woven. The parade proceeds daily in most industries; the child who says so is still hiring.
